## How to use this document

You are filling the required-content inventory for two platforms. Treat the checklist as law. Do not invent copy for items marked **not answerable**. Do not paraphrase attached copy into a new voice. Where copy exists and the item is still short of target length or lives at the wrong URL, **place the attached copy first**, then write only the missing remainder.

Rules:

1. Attached copy is the canonical existing text. Quote it, move it, or extend it. Do not replace it with a rewrite unless the item is explicitly marked *thin / needs expansion*.
2. Green items are required. Amber items are recommended and can wait.
3. Movemental public copy is agent-first: `/` redirects to `/agent`. Many inventory URLs (`/pathway`, `/pricing`, `/faq`, `/contact`, `/check`) are not live routes. Attached copy often lives on an agent screen. When you publish the inventory URL, move this copy there; do not write a second version.
4. Stage naming in live Movemental copy is **Safety · Sandbox · Training · Tech**. The inventory uses **Safety · Sandbox · Skills · Solutions**. Keep the live names unless a later canon decision changes them. Do not mix both on one page.
5. Josh Shepherd live copy lives in `movement-leader-websites/josh-shepherd`. Unpublished essays live in that repo at `docs/article-export/`. Movemental long-form also lives at `docs/articles/` and `/research`.
6. Word counts in the checklist are targets. Attached copy that is short of target still counts as existing — expand, do not start over.
7. Named case studies with permission and numbers: **not answerable** on either platform. Do not reconstruct one from founder bios.

Status keys used below:

# Part A — movemental.ai

Inventory label: movemental.ai. Live host: agent-first (`/` → `/agent`). Copy SSOTs are named under each item.

## Personas (from the checklist — keep these in view when placing copy)

**01 · The leader who suspects and has not looked** · Primary buyer · pastor, ED, president  
Wants: a sensible position on AI. Something defensible. Ideally something short.  
Needs: to find out the decision has already been made by default, one staff member at a time, and that what they have is not a policy or a ban but private habits leadership cannot see. Second: a floor rather than a program. Naming that the first step is small and cheap is what makes the rest credible.  
Loses them: manufactured urgency. Compliance language. Anything treating the AI question as separable from their mission.

**02 · The one who has to defend it** · Fiduciary · board chair, finance director, provost  
Wants: evidence, references, and a clear price.  
Needs: to see that their existing duties have expanded rather than that a new risk has appeared. Fiduciary continuity is the reframe that converts a skeptic into an internal advocate. Second: to see you decline to sell something.  
Loses them: an unsourced statistic. A price that turns out to be negotiable. Any gap between a stated commitment and an observed practice.

**03 · The prospective Movement Voice** · Underwriter · senior leader being invited  
Wants: to understand the offer, the commitment, and what it costs them in time.  
Needs: to see who else is in and how they got there. The selection standard matters more than the compensation, because compensation is a contract and the standard is the risk. Second: proof of sovereignty over their own corpus.  
Loses them: being paid in logos and exposure. Any suggestion they are a testimonial. Finding someone in the network they would not have vouched for.

## 01 · Recognition layer · The recognition instrument

- **Required.** Type: Interactive self-check · no email gate. Length: 5 questions · 60–120 words framing. Location: Home hero · `/check`.
- **Status:** Partial. There is no `/check`. The live instrument is a **6-beat** Organizational Reality Map in the agent room (`toBeat`). `/assess` is a magic-link email gate into that room — the inventory says no email gate.
- **Sources:** `src/lib/agent-room/data/home-copy.ts`, `src/lib/agent-room/data/beat-catalog.ts`, `src/app/assess/page.tsx`

### Attached — home framing (81 words)

Navigate AI without eroding the trust you spent decades building.

We help mission-driven organizations respond to AI without losing the trust their work depends on, through one simple path: use AI safely, experiment to find valuable, ethical use cases, train your people in AI leadership and maturity, and then build custom technological solutions tailor-made for your organization.

Built with and backed by movement leaders including Alan Hirsch, Brad Brisco, JR Woodward, Dave Ferguson, Josh Shepherd, and others in the network.

Lead chip: Get a clear next AI step.

### Attached — `/assess` door copy (too gated for this item; keep for item 03)

Find out the truth about AI in your organization.

A short, honest reality check, no sales pitch. Enter your email and we'll send a one-tap link into the room where you'll map where your organization actually stands.

### Attached — the six beats (live instrument)

**Beat 1 · Start.** First — what kind of organization are you?  
Church / Nonprofit / Seminary or institution / Something else.

**Beat 2 · Sandbox.** Is AI already being used in your actual work — emails, donor letters, lesson plans, sermons, grants?  
Yes, definitely / Probably, but I'm not sure / No, not yet.

**Beat 3 · Safety.** Could your senior leadership, right now, name every AI tool your staff uses — and what goes into each one?  
Yes, all of it / Some of it / Honestly, no.

**Beat 4 · Safety (gate).** Has someone with the authority to decide actually decided what's okay — in writing, where staff can find it before they guess?  
Yes — written and ratified / We've talked about it / No.

**Beat 5 · Training.** If a donor, parishioner, or board member learned tomorrow exactly how AI is used in your work — would it strengthen their trust, or shake it?  
Strengthen it / Not sure / Shake it.

**Beat 6a · Safety (if gate passed).** Does it name specific things you refuse to do with AI — or is it general guidance?  
Names specific refusals / It's more general.

**Beat 6b · Last (if gate failed).** Last one — what are you most worried about getting wrong?  
Trust with the people we serve / A data or privacy breach / Staff using it badly / Falling behind / Not sure yet.

**Still needed:** a 5-question ungated `/check` whose only job is one sentence the leader would not have written that morning. The visibility beat is the closest to that job. Do not replace these questions with a lead-qualifying quiz.

## 04 · Argument layer · The Path, as page and as essay

- **Required.** Type: Methodology hub + long-form essay. Length: 1,200–2,000 hub · 3,500–5,000 essay. Location: `/pathway` · `/the-path`.
- **Status:** Partial. Live hub is the agent Path screen (~200–300 words). No `/the-path`. Closest long copy: research/articles on fragmentation, credibility, and the four-stage order. Archive hub ~1,145 words; archive ThePathPage ~1,894 — both under the essay target and not live.

### Attached — live Path hub

One ordered path. It starts with Safety.

The order is not arbitrary. Safety first, because AI is already in the room. Sandbox before Training before Tech. Handing powerful tools to people who cannot yet steward them is replacement, not progress.

**01 Safety.** Name what AI may and may not do in your mission. Your AI Safety Charter, ratified by your board, before anything else.  
Acceptable use, data boundaries, and theological red lines, written down and adopted before anyone builds on sand.

**02 Sandbox.** Try AI against real work, in a bounded place. Sort what helps from what doesn't.  
Your team runs trials inside the charter you ratified. Each use case goes green, yellow, or red. You leave with a Future Plan leadership can sign.

**03 Training.** Form the people who will carry it. Judgment, not a one-off workshop.  
An eight-week cohort building discernment, authorship, and stewardship in the leaders who will steward AI inside your organization.

**04 Tech.** Build what your work actually needs, on what you already decided and tested.  
Scoped deployment, from improving tools you already use to network-scale work. Only after clear rules, real trials, and formed people.

### Attached — sector path intros (same argument, three framings)

**Churches.** We don't start with the tech. There's an order. Safety first, decide in writing what you will and won't do with AI, including pastoral care boundaries and disclosure. Then Sandbox, test against real ministry work. Then Training, form your people. Then Tech, build the tools. Your first move is Safety.

**Nonprofits.** We don't start with the tech. There's an order. Safety first: a ratified AI Safety Charter your board can sign, covering acceptable use, data handling, disclosure, and incident response. Then Sandbox, where you test AI against real work. Then Training, where you form your team. Then Tech, where you build the tools. Your first move is Safety. Each step earns the next. Skip one, and the ones after it have nothing to stand on.

**Institutions.** We don't do this all at once, and we don't start with the tech. There's an order. Safety first, decide in writing what you will and won't do with AI. Then Sandbox, test it against real work. Then Training, form your people. Then Tech, build the tools. Each step earns the next. Your first move is Safety.

### Attached — Safety (`src/components/agent-room/screen/stub/safety-screen.tsx`)

Stage 01 · Safety

Your team is already using AI. No one has said what's allowed.

Safety is the first step on the path. Before you build anything, you decide out loud and on the record what AI may and may not do in your mission.

**Why this comes first.** For a business, an AI mistake costs efficiency. For a church, a nonprofit, or a seminary, it costs trust. A sermon quietly written by a machine. Donor records pasted into a consumer tool. A cloned voice asking your people for money. None of these are hypothetical. None are efficiency problems. They are credibility problems. Credibility is your product. There is no second product to fall back on.

91% of church leaders support using AI in ministry. Most use it weekly.  
9% have written any policy for it.  
60% are concerned about cloned-voice fraud, and 1 in 4 say AI scams have already reached their community.

The tools arrived. The decisions did not. Safety closes that gap before it costs you.

**What changes the day you ratify.** The value arrives the moment your board says yes. From that point you have a clear answer for a journalist. An answer a major donor can trust. One shared frame for your whole staff. A document you can point to when a vendor pitches something you already decided against. You stop reacting to AI and start leading through it.

**What it produces.** One thing: your AI Safety Charter. Five plain layers your board can ratify.

01 Statement — what we believe about AI in our mission.  
02 Policy — what we will do, and what we refuse.  
03 Context — what is actually true in our environment right now.  
04 Rules — what governs AI use in specific areas.  
05 Response Plans — what we do when something goes wrong.

Inside those five layers are seven short, practical documents, including your AI use charter, your data-handling standards, your disclosure standard, and your response plan for a cloned voice. Nothing bloated. The smallest set that actually protects you.

**Two ways forward.** We are not trying to talk you out of the free route. Both produce the same ratified Charter. The only difference is who holds the pen, and how fast you get there.

Free, and we guide you. Free · about 1 to 2 months. Complete Safety yourself with the handbook, *It Starts With Safety*. Your team drafts all five layers, and we point the way when you need it. Best if you have the time, the alignment, and the discipline to finish.

Build your dashboard. Free to start · no call, no checkout. We draft all five layers to your organization. You review, edit, and ratify inside your dashboard. Help is one click away if you want it.

### Attached — Sandbox

Stage 02 · Sandbox

Safety told you what's allowed. Sandbox is where you find out what's valuable.

Your team tries AI against real work, inside the rules your board already ratified. Each use case gets sorted green, yellow, or red. You leave with a Future Plan your leadership can actually sign.

**Why this comes second.** Safety without Sandbox is barriers built before anyone tested whether the tools had value. Sandbox without Safety is reckless. You need the charter first. Then you need honest trials against your own work, not a vendor demo.

A generic AI workshop can teach prompts. It cannot tell you which uses fit your mission, your data, or your people. That sorting happens here, against material your team already carries.

**What it produces.** Three things your board can read. A Future Plan with green, yellow, and red use cases. A Discernment Memo naming what you learned and now believe is true. A Readiness Assessment recommending whether to move to Training.

The free field guide walks eight phases, from boundaries through ethics review to the Future Plan. The facilitated path adds in-person teaching, a recipe library tuned to your work, and dashboard integration with your Safety charter.

(Pricing for this stage is attached under item 13/14.)

### Attached — Training (inventory: Skills)

Stage 03 · Training

Training transfers technique. Formation reshapes judgment.

Training is an eight-week cohort for the people who will carry AI decisions inside your organization. Not staff who learned a tool. Leaders who can name the line, defend authorship, and steward what you already decided in Safety and tested in Sandbox.

**Why this comes third.** Sandbox gives you findings. Training gives you people who can carry them. Handing powerful tools to a team that has not been formed is replacement, not progress. AI does not do the discernment, the relationships, or the care. Your people do. This stage forms them.

A one-day workshop can teach prompts. It cannot form judgment about when AI should not touch pastoral notes, donor letters, or student records. That work needs peers, time, and your organization's own material on the table.

**What it builds.** Three capacities, practiced together over eight weeks. Discernment: reading AI output against your real work and naming when it is confidently wrong. Authorship: knowing when AI helped and when it crossed into writing under your name. Stewardship: holding the care boundaries from your charter when a vendor or a staff member pushes past them.

The curriculum anchors to your own ratified Statement and Policy from Safety. Certification rests on demonstrated capacity, not attendance.

The paid cohort runs today through Movemental's LMS. The free field guide ships when it's ready.

### Attached — Tech (inventory: Solutions)

Stage 04 · Tech

Build only after the people and the rules are ready.

Tech is scoped AI deployment inside your organization. Built by formed people. Governed by a working charter. Aimed at use cases your Sandbox already sorted green or yellow. Not a tech purchase to skip the first three stages.

**Why this comes last.** Enterprise Copilot with good prompts may be enough. If your Sandbox Future Plan says so, start there. We will tell you when a lighter path fits. Tech is for when the work needs custom workflows, shared content, or network-scale coordination that off-the-shelf tools cannot carry honestly.

Deploying AI into hands that cannot steward it, inside rules nobody has ratified, is how trust erodes while the dashboard looks impressive. The order is not upsell. It is the smallest honest sequence.

**Modular builds.** Tech is built in layers on top of your ratified foundation. Foundation is included in every platform. Add the modules your organization needs.

Foundation — Built in. The spine of every platform: website, accounts, library, governance, and AI assistant. Included in every Tech engagement.  
Publishing — $30,000. Your public face and the tools to run it, with full agentic implementation custom to your organization.  
Formation — $30,000. Courses, cohorts, and learning paths — how you form and teach people inside your platform.  
Relationships — $30,000. People, giving, and operations in one place — donor stewardship, member care, and staff workflows.

Every stage has a free field guide. Tech's guide is in progress.

Questions about fit or scope? Get in touch. We would rather name a smaller first step than sell a build you are not ready to operate.

### Attached — churches pain section

Here's what's already happening. None of this was planned. It's just true right now.

**AI is already in the study, with no rule about the pulpit.** Many pastors already use AI for research or a first draft. Few have decided, in writing, what that means for teaching from the pulpit. About four in ten Protestant pastors now use AI for ministry, and only one in twenty churches has a formal policy for it. The practice arrived years ahead of the agreement.

**Pastoral care notes are in the wrong place.** Staff paste counseling and care notes into consumer AI tools with no standard for what is kept or who can see it. AI does not do pastoral care, and these notes should never be in those tools. No one decided this. It is just where the work landed when there was nowhere safer to put it.

**People cannot always tell what is really you.** When a member cannot tell whether you wrote it, a volunteer drafted it, or it was generated, trust erodes a little. Most people now say it matters whether something was made by a person or by AI, and most are not confident they can tell the difference. That gap is exactly where a church's credibility leaks.

**Your people are already asking the machine.** Nearly one in three U.S. adults now say spiritual advice from AI is as trustworthy as advice from a pastor, and among Gen Z and Millennials it is two in five. Meanwhile only twelve percent of pastors say they feel ready to teach about AI at all. Your younger members are asking the questions they used to bring to a mentor, and getting answers from a model trained by someone else.

**A model does not share your church's convictions.** The general-purpose models your members ask are not neutral on faith. Independent testing found they score lowest of all on questions of Christian worldview. When your congregation asks the machine instead of asking you, they are not getting your church's theology back. They are getting an average of the internet's.

**Your voice can be cloned, and it is already happening.** A few minutes of sermon footage is enough to fake a pastor's voice and use it to solicit emergency gifts from members. This is not hypothetical. Voice-cloning fraud rose more than four hundred percent year over year, and faith leaders are being impersonated specifically because their people trust their voice.

These aren't six problems. They're one.

Underneath all of it is fragmentation. Your teaching lives in sermons no one can search. Hard-won wisdom lives in founders' heads, one bus accident away from being lost. You know your people in pieces. You can't see your own congregation whole.

What is true of one writer's scattered work is true of a church's scattered body. The teaching was whole in your people. It lives in video archives, bulletins, and notebooks that do not speak to each other.

AI built on top of that doesn't pull the pieces together. By default it reflects the scatter back, faster and louder, wearing your name without carrying your person. That's not a tech glitch. It's what happens when the foundation is broken.

Young adults are watching most closely. They're asking the machine the questions they used to ask the church. They're waiting to see whether you have anything true to say in this moment, or whether you'll answer with fear, or a shrug.

**The full case, in one letter.** Here's the whole argument in plain words, written for your pastor and elders. Read it here, or download it to share.

**We gather what's scattered into one place.** Movemental takes your people, your teaching, and your record and gathers them into one connected foundation, one place your church owns. Visible to your elders. Verifiable for your congregation. Built from what's actually yours, not a generic chatbot trained on the open web.

Sermons were unsearchable → now your teaching is findable and grounded in your own words.  
Your voice could be faked → now there's a verified record of what's really yours.  
Staff used AI without approval → now there's a ratified AI Charter everyone can follow.  
Members couldn't tell who wrote what → now disclosure and authorship are clear, in writing.

**Then we build the tools on top of it.** The working platform, on the desk and in your pocket. Pick a layer, open any piece. Which is usually where a fair question comes up, the one every pastor asks when the price lands: so isn't this just an expensive church website?

**But tools alone aren't the answer.** Tech without formed people isn't discipleship. It's replacement. Hand powerful tools to a staff that hasn't been formed to steward them, and you get the failure mode everyone is already living through.

The tools come with formation. Discernment stays with your leaders. Authorship keeps a real human behind the words. Stewardship cares for what's been entrusted to you. AI does not do pastoral care. For a church, this isn't an add-on. It's the work.

A generation of young adults is deciding, from what they watch you do, whether the church has anything true to say in this moment. Formation is how you answer them. Not with a policy PDF alone, but with people who can lead through this carefully.

Hand line: Formation isn't extra. It's the point.

**Start with a conversation.** Churches don't start this with a checkout button. They start with a talk. Tell us where you are, and we'll show you the first step. The letter above is yours to share with your elders while you decide.

To a Lead Pastor

I want to begin with something already happening inside your church, whether or not anyone decided it should.

Right now someone on your staff is using AI. They are drafting an email with it, summarizing a meeting, or writing the first version of a sermon outline that will go out under your name. A few are pasting things into these tools they should not be pasting: pastoral notes, member details, counseling summaries. Almost none are checking the result against a policy, because almost no church has written one. Nobody invited any of this. It simply arrived. It is here now.

And the people watching most closely are young adults. Their feelings about all of this split nearly down the middle, half hopeful and half wary. They are asking the machine the questions they used to ask a mentor. How do I make sense of my life. How do I actually disciple people. What is the church even for. They are waiting to see whether the church has anything true to say in this moment, or whether it will answer with fear, or with a shrug.

And the thing most at risk is the very thing you exist to protect. For a business, an AI mistake loses a client; there is another client. For a church, credibility is not an advantage. It is the product. When a member cannot tell whether you wrote it, voice-cloned it, or a volunteer drafted it, trust erodes quietly. Voice cloning and impersonation are no longer theoretical. Scammers harvest sermon footage and livestreams to clone pastors' voices and solicit emergency gifts. Your name no longer proves it is really you.

Underneath that exposure sits the same deeper wound every church carries. Your teaching lives in sermons no one can search. Your hard-won, practiced wisdom lives in the founders' heads, one bus accident away from being lost. You know your people in fragments and cannot see your own body whole. AI built on top of that does not pull the pieces together. By default it reflects the scatter back, faster, louder, wearing your name without carrying your person.

So let me tell you what we do, and why the order of it matters.

The work has a sequence. Safety comes first, because AI is already in the room. Before anything else, a church needs a short AI Charter your elders can sign: what you believe about this, what you will do, what you refuse to do, pastoral care boundaries, disclosure when AI was used, and what you do when something goes wrong. This is not consulting overhead. It is a small step against costs you are already paying without naming them. After Safety comes Sandbox, where a team tests AI against real ministry work and decides honestly what helps, what is risky, and what is off limits. Then Training, where a group inside the church builds the capacities this work demands: discernment, authorship, care. Then Tech, where AI is integrated into how the church runs, last, because handing powerful tools to people who cannot yet use them wisely is not discipleship but replacement. We order the rebuild so it does not destroy the thing it was meant to serve.

Here is the gift hidden in your particular weight. Do this work, and you do not only protect your congregation. You answer the generation asking the machine the questions they used to ask the church, not with a shrug, but with people who can lead through this carefully.

I will be plain about why this is possible now. We use the tools we sell on ourselves, first. We do not use AI to author anything under a human's name. We are not the platform; the people and their work are the platform, and they own it. Start with Safety. We can facilitate it with you, or you can complete it on your own with the free handbook.

I will end where this really comes from. A generation of young adults is deciding, from what they watch you do, whether the church has anything true to say in this moment. Begin where it begins. Decide, in writing, what you will and will not do, while you still have room to choose together.

### Attached — nonprofits pain section

Here's what's already happening. None of this was planned. It's just true right now.

**AI is already inside your organization.** Your staff are not waiting for a policy. Ninety-two percent of nonprofits already use AI in some form, and most of that use is one person, one personal account, one task at a time. The tools arrived before the decision did.

**Donor records are sitting in tools you do not control.** Someone on your team pastes donor and beneficiary details into a personal AI account to clean up a list or draft an appeal. There is no contract, no retention rule, and no one ever decided this was allowed. It is not negligence. It is what happens when 81% of the work runs through individual accounts with no shared place to do it safely.

**Your board has not met its duty yet.** Nearly half of nonprofits have no AI governance policy at all. The board's job to oversee how the organization handles risk now includes this, whether or not anything has gone wrong so far. The duty applies before the harm, not after it.

**The time you are saving is not adding up.** Most teams report small gains from AI and little that compounds. Across nonprofit, enterprise, and faith-sector studies, only five to seven percent of organizations see real capability improvement, and almost all of them have one thing in common: they redesigned how the work flows, instead of bolting AI onto the old steps. Individual use never adds up to organizational strength on its own.

**Your mission voice is drifting, quietly.** The loud risk is a data breach. The quiet one is worse, because no one notices it for a year. Appeals start to sound generic. Reports round off the inconvenient detail. The specific, particular voice that made donors trust you gets sanded down a draft at a time, until your organization reads like every other organization.

**Every staff departure takes memory with it.** A mid-tier donor who gave steadily for seven years drifts away, because the only person who knew them left, and the relationship lived in that person's head and inbox, not in anything the organization kept. It is one donor, then another. A slow leak no dashboard catches. This is not a generosity problem. It is a memory problem.

These aren't six problems. They're one.

Underneath the governance gap is fragmentation. Your program knowledge lives in scattered documents. Your donor relationships sit in silos. Your mission voice gets rewritten a dozen different ways by a dozen different staff. None of it is connected. None of it is owned as one record.

What's true of one leader's scattered life-work is true of an organization's scattered record. The work was whole in the mission. It lives in pieces across grants, decks, and inboxes, and most of your people will never do the dig.

AI built on that foundation doesn't fix the scatter. It multiplies it. Faster drafts of the wrong story. Quicker research with no shared standard. Individual shortcuts that never become something the whole organization can use.

The quieter harm isn't a headline breach. It's the slow erosion of mission integrity. Appeals that subtly mischaracterize the program. Reports that round off the inconvenient detail. Outreach lists that deprioritize the very people your mission was designed to serve.

**The full case, in one letter.** Here's the whole argument in plain words, written for your board. Read it here, or download it to send.

**We gather what's scattered into one place.** Movemental takes your people, your program record, and your mission voice and gathers them into one connected foundation. A single source of truth your organization owns. It's visible to leadership. It's verifiable for donors. And it's built from what's actually yours.

Donor data was exposed → now data-handling standards are ratified and enforceable.  
Reports drifted from mission → now drafts are grounded in your own verified record.  
Staff used AI without approval → now there's an AI Safety Charter your board can sign.  
Capability never compounded → now shared workflows turn individual use into organizational strength.

**But tools alone aren't the answer.** Tech without formed people isn't progress. It's replacement. Boards that buy tools without forming staff get unapproved AI at scale, faster.

So the tools come with formation. Discernment for leadership. Authorship for anything that goes out under your name. Stewardship for donor and beneficiary trust. For a nonprofit, fiduciary duty and mission integrity depend on both.

Your constituents are watching whether you lead through this moment with care, or whether AI becomes one more invisible shortcut that slowly misrepresents the work you've been entrusted to do.

Do you start with software? No. Safety comes first, governance and policy before deployment. We do not sell tools or begin with a build.  
Do you replace human judgment with AI? No. AI assists; humans decide. Formation and oversight protocols are built before any custom assistant ships.  
Do you treat efficiency as the highest goal? No. Wisdom is slower than recklessness. Clarity and alignment create long-term acceleration; shortcuts fracture culture.  
Do you take referral fees, sponsorships, or affiliate revenue from AI vendors? No. You pay vendors directly. We remain vendor-agnostic with no hidden incentives.  
Will you walk away from an engagement that is not a fit? Yes. If we are not the right partner, we will say so plainly rather than take work we cannot stand behind.

## 12 · Commitment layer · How we use AI on ourselves

- **Required.** Type: Position page. Length: 1,000–1,600. Location: `/how-we-use-ai` (live: `/agent/how-we-use-ai`).
- **Status:** Attached. In range if you count data + experience. Also article `docs/articles/how-movemental-uses-ai.md`.

### Attached — full live page copy

**Hero.** How we use AI  
We use the tools we sell. On ourselves, first.

We do not ask organizations to do anything we have not done. Every guardrail we ask a leader or a board to ratify, we have built into our own work first. This page is where we name what we refuse, how we sort use cases, and what we will not build, so anyone reading the site knows where we stand.

Most public AI discourse splits into “AI is a savior” or “AI is a threat.” We reject both. AI surfaces and amplifies what humans have already produced, and how a person reacts to it often reveals their underlying view of human nature. Our work starts from a simpler operational rule: if AI mirrors the humans it is around, govern the humans, the corpus, and the relationships first.

**Our commitments.** What we will not do, ever.  
These are not preferences. They are the line. Breaking one would cost the exact trust we exist to protect.

No manufactured urgency or scarcity. We will never manufacture a deadline or a fear of missing out to move you.

No faked authorship. We help your people tell their own story. We never write under a human's name as if it were them.

AI gathers and drafts. Humans discern, care, and speak. AI does the gathering and the drafting. It never does the discernment, the shepherding, the relationships, or the care.

We claim only what is earned. We do not promise outcomes the work has not produced yet. If a number appears on this site, it has a footnote.

Extra care wherever vulnerable people are involved. When you serve minors or families, we are more cautious, not less.

**What we refuse.** Three lines we do not cross.  
These refusals are essential, not ethics bolted onto a product after the fact. They shape every line of code we ship and every document we help produce.

Replacement of relationship. We do not use AI to simulate pastoral presence, mentoring, or care. Formation happens in relationship. AI can support the work around that relationship; it cannot be the relationship.

Formation without presence. We do not hand over the work that forms us. Preaching, teaching, and writing that carries our convictions go to the machine only with our full engagement. If it goes out under our name and is meant to form people, we have read it, weighed it, and owned it.

Amplification without credibility. We do not use AI to look bigger than the work and network actually warrant. Not more output, more polish, or more reach when we have not done the work or do not have the people to back it up. Looking more credible than you are fails when it outruns the credibility you actually have.

**Green / yellow / red.** How we sort use cases.  
Not all AI use is equivalent. This is the same framework we use in Safety and Sandbox engagements, and how we evaluate our own use internally.

Green light. Clear human benefit, no meaningful negative consequence.  
Structure, findability, admin, and translation. These are tasks that do not require your voice or your judgment. First drafts you will edit and own before anything goes out under your name. AI handles the supporting work; you stay in the loop where the output represents you.  
Examples: Making existing work searchable. Metadata, headings, internal linking. Translating work you have already written. Formatting and administrative repetition.

Yellow light. Real benefit, but only with guardrails.  
Context-dependent. A quick internal summary is not the same as a public-facing piece. A first draft you will heavily edit is not the same as a post you publish with light changes. When in doubt, slow down. When the output will form people or represent you publicly, the human in the loop is you, reading, weighing, owning.  
Examples: Drafts you review before sending. Research where citation and verification are required. Facilitated conversations where AI never substitutes for participants.

Red light. Harm, regardless of how carefully it is deployed.  
The lines we do not cross, and the lines we help organizations name in Safety. AI used to author content under a human's name without disclosure. AI impersonating humans in pastoral or counseling contexts. AI making eligibility decisions that affect people's access to services. We do not deploy these. We help the organizations we work with publicly commit to refusing them as well.  
Examples: Undisclosed authorship under a human name. Pastoral or counseling impersonation. Decisions about access to care or services.

**You stay in charge.** AI supports your credibility, it does not replace you.

The sustainable pattern: you handle creation and authority, what you teach, what you write, what you put your name on. AI handles discoverability and circulation: structure, metadata, translation, formatting, linking. Your work becomes easier to find and connect without the machine becoming you.

AI is trained on the broad output of human writing, speech, and behavior. When you interact with it, it mirrors and amplifies what it has been trained on, and it mirrors and amplifies you specifically. That is why the most important operational decision is not which model you pick. It is who you deliberately gather around the work: the humans whose corpus, judgment, and vouching the system will reflect back.

AI can help your work be legible and connected. It never becomes you. Only people can vouch for you. Only you can mean what you say before God and stand answerable for it as true.

Hand line: You out front. AI in the background.

**The scenius refusals.** What we will not build into the network.  
The extractive version of this business is obvious, and we are building against it. That includes product choices, not only policy statements.

No ranked leaderboards.  
No vanity metrics.  
No engagement-optimized feeds.  
No parasocial substitutes where reading replaces relationship.

If a feature would feel extractive to us as members, we don't ship it.

## 22 · Entry layer · About and founders

### Attached — About Movemental (full live document copy)

**Who we are.**  
We help you meet AI without losing the trust your work depends on.

Movemental builds the platform mission-driven organizations need to meet AI with their integrity intact. We gather your scattered work into one place, make it verifiable, build the tools on top of it, and help you govern the whole thing. We go in order, and the order starts with Safety.

We serve churches, nonprofits, seminaries, and the individual leaders whose body of work is worth protecting.

Movemental, founded 2026. Built out of a two-year conversation among three people who could not stop talking about what AI was doing to the institutions, and the trust, they love.

**Why we exist.**  
The problem underneath the problem is fragmentation.

A leader's life-work, or an institution's, was whole in the living of it. Then it scattered. Into books and talks and decks and inboxes and a few people's memories. Most of it is real, and almost none of it is gathered. That is fragmentation, and it was a quiet problem until AI arrived.

AI did not cause the scatter. It is a mirror. Pointed at fragmented work, it multiplies the fragments. It fills the gaps with something fluent and wrong, faster than anyone can correct it. The result is a world where a reader can no longer tell what is real, who actually said it, or whether it is trustworthy at all.

So the work now is credibility. Not louder marketing. The ability to be believed, and to be the answer the machine returns when someone asks about you. That is downstream of one thing: having gathered your real work into something coherent and verifiable. Coherence is the task, but not all coherence heals. We build toward the kind that does.

**The story.**  
It started as a conversation.

For two years, Josh kept circling the same worry with Alan and Brad. AI was arriving in churches, nonprofits, and seminaries faster than anyone was deciding how to meet it. The people most exposed were the ones whose entire work rests on trust, and they had the least time to think it through.

Josh did not want to add to the noise. He wanted to build the thing he wished existed: a way for a mission-driven organization to meet this moment in order, without faking its way through, and without losing the human core of the work. Alan and Brad joined, opened the authorship question together, and the conversation became a partnership. In 2026, it became Movemental.

**How we use AI (about version).**  
We use the tools on ourselves first.

We do not sell anything we will not use. This site, our research, and our own agents are built the way we would build yours. We hold ourselves to the same Safety standard we ask of you, and we write our own AI Charter before we help you write yours.

When we get it wrong, we say so. When we are early, we say that too. The point is not to look more finished than we are. It is to be the kind of organization you can actually trust with this.

Your data. We treat your work as yours. We do not train models on it, we are clear about where it lives and who can see it, and the data-handling standards we help you ratify are the ones we hold ourselves. Trust is the product, so the way we handle your data is the proof.

**What we refuse.** Some things we won't do, ever.  
These are not preferences. They are the line. Breaking one would cost the exact trust we exist to protect.

No urgency, no scarcity, no pressure. We will never manufacture a deadline or a fear of missing out to move you.  
We never fake authorship. We help your people tell their own story. We never write under a human's name as if it were them.  
We never replace the sacred. AI does the gathering and the drafting. It never does the discernment, the shepherding, the relationships, or the care.  
We claim only what is earned. We do not promise outcomes the work has not produced yet.  
We take extra care with the vulnerable. When you serve minors or families, we are more cautious, not less.

**The founders.** Three people who couldn't stop talking about it.

**Who did what.** Alan Hirsch is the movement thinker. Brad Brisco is the missional leader and CEO. Josh Shepherd is the technical founder who builds the platform, the agents, and the system underneath.

Brad holds the CEO seat on purpose. Trust is the product, and he already carries that trust in the field. The org chart says the thesis: the person who builds hands the trust seat to the person who already holds it.

**Talk to us.** Start with a conversation.  
No checkout button. No pressure. Tell us where your organization is, and we will show you the first step, which is almost always Safety, and almost always free to begin.

Everything on this page is sourced, attributed, and verifiable. That is the point.

### Attached — Alan Hirsch (full profile body)

Alan Hirsch is the missiologist who coined the term movemental, the namesake of this platform, and built the intellectual architecture much of the contemporary missional church now runs on. Born in Johannesburg in 1959, raised in apartheid-era South Africa, he emigrated to Australia in 1983 and pastored the South Melbourne Restoration Community for fifteen years among addicts, sex workers, and the chronically housed before turning that ministry's lessons into theory.

His magnum opus, The Forgotten Ways (Brazos, 2006), introduced the mDNA framework and the concept of Apostolic Genius; 5Q (2017) and The Permanent Revolution (Jossey-Bass, 2012, with Tim Catchim) have made APEST one of the most widely adopted readings of Ephesians 4 in the Western church, with more than 150,000 assessments taken through his platforms. Across twenty books published with seven publishers, including The Shaping of Things to Come with Michael Frost, ReJesus, Untamed with Debra Hirsch, and Metanoia with Rob Kelly, he has built a coherent line from Christology through missiology to ecclesiology.

He founded 100Movements, co-founded the Forge Mission Training Network and 5Q Collective, and co-founded the M.A. in Missional Church Movements at Wheaton College. He teaches as adjunct faculty at Fuller, George Fox, and Asbury, and works as embedded consultant for Redeemer City to City and movement mentor for NewThing International.

### Attached — Brad Brisco (full profile body)

Brad Brisco works the seam most missional writers avoid: the seam between post-Christendom theology and a Southern Baptist denominational system. As Director of Multiplication Strategies for Send Network at the North American Mission Board, he translates Newbigin, Bosch, Frost, and Hirsch into the planting language of a tradition that has not always reached for them. He earned a D.Min. in Missional Ecclesiology with a dissertation on helping existing congregations transition toward mission, and he has carried that question into eighteen-plus years of college teaching across History of Christianity, Theology of Place, and Launching Apostolic Movements.

His written corpus moves in stages alongside Lance Ford, from the small-group curriculum Missional Essentials, through The Missional Quest (InterVarsity Press) and Next Door As It Is In Heaven (NavPress, 2016), to ReThink and his solo synthesis Covocational Church Planting (Missional Press, 2021), released as a free bilingual ebook in English and Spanish. He co-founded Forge Kansas City and the Sentralized Conference, sits on the Forge America national leadership team, and writes regularly across New Churches, ChurchLeaders.com, and his own missionalchurchnetwork.com.

At Movemental, Brad holds the CEO seat. Trust is the product, and he already carries that trust in the field — decades of denominational and network-level missional work, teaching, and writing alongside Alan Hirsch.

### Attached — Josh Shepherd (full profile body)

Josh Shepherd is a founder of Movemental, LLC (movemental.ai), alongside Alan Hirsch and Brad Brisco. Movemental was founded in 2026, out of a two-year conversation among the three of them about what AI was doing to the institutions, and the trust, they care about.

Within that trio, Josh is the technical founder. Alan is the movement thinker. Brad is the missional leader. Josh is the one who builds. He designs and writes the platform, the agents, and the system underneath, so the ideas become something an organization can actually use. He is based in Kansas City.

Josh came to this work from inside it: years as a Methodist pastor, then founding a neomonastic, communal nonprofit where he and his wife lived alongside young adults in extended residency. From direct service through neighborhood ministry and into product work, he has built AI tools for real organizations serving real families — including bilingual youth work where the stakes are children and trust, not theory.

Movemental helps churches, nonprofits, seminaries, institutions, and individual movement leaders meet AI without losing the trust their work depends on. Josh holds the whole vision, not just the engineering. The company is agent-first: the homepage is an agent, not a brochure. The path goes in order — Safety, Sandbox, Training, Tech — because building tools for people who have not decided their boundaries just automates the mess faster.

He writes plainly, refuses hype, and is unusually scrupulous about claiming only what is true. He would rather show you a thing than describe it, and he would rather be early and honest than finished and false.

Trust line: Josh is Founder and CTO and architect of the platform. He handed the CEO seat to Brad on purpose: trust is the product, and Brad already carries that trust in the field.

Alan Hirsch (Co-Founder and Chief Movement Officer), Brad Brisco (Co-Founder and CEO), and Josh Shepherd (Founder and CTO). The full story is on About; full bios live at /about/alan-hirsch, /about/brad-brisco, and /about/josh-shepherd.

Who is the CEO, and why Brad?  
Brad Brisco is CEO. Trust is the product, and he already carries that trust in the field — decades of denominational and network-level missional work alongside Alan. Josh, who builds the platform, handed the CEO seat to Brad on purpose.

Who is Josh Shepherd?  
Josh is Founder and CTO. He designs and builds the platform, the agents, and the system underneath. He started the two-year conversation that became Movemental in 2026. His full profile is at /about/josh-shepherd.

**Getting started**

What should we do first? Start with Safety. Reach out via our Contact page to schedule a diagnostic call.  
Do we need technical expertise to begin? No. The Movemental Path begins with leadership alignment, not software engineering.  
Is this a tool, a course, or a consulting engagement? It is consulting with a clear method behind it. See Ways to Engage on the Contact page.  
What does the first call look like? Thirty minutes mapping your specific friction points without any sales pressure.  
How do we know if we are ready? If your staff is already using ChatGPT implicitly, you are ready, because you are already exposed.  
Do we need to have an AI strategy already? No. We help you build something that lasts rather than a strategy that falls apart under pressure.

**The four stages, in order**

What is the Movemental Path? Movemental's public methodology, four stages in order: Safety, Sandbox, Training, Tech. Read the Path summary for the full arc.  
Why this order? Why not all four in parallel? Attempting tech before safety opens you to data breaches. Changing the order collapses the required human formation.  
Can we skip stages if we have already done some of this? We will audit any work you've done. If it holds up, we move forward. Most organizations discover gaps in their safety foundation.  
Do the stages overlap? Yes, in time. But you cannot start the next stage until the one before it is actually done.  
What does Safety actually cover? Acceptable use policies, data boundary definitions, and theological red lines: your AI Charter, ratified before anything else.  
What does Sandbox mean in practice? Isolated environments where staff can securely learn prompts and limits without risking public trust or constituent data.  
What do Training and Tech include? Training forms human judgment. Tech is building AI into your actual workflows, only after safety and skill are in place.

**Approach and philosophy**

Is Movemental pro-AI or anti-AI? We are pro-mission. We treat AI as an inevitably disruptive change that must be stewarded deliberately rather than accepted universally.  
Why not just start using tools? Because tools shape the people who use them. Untethered tool usage fractures organizational culture.  
Is this primarily a technology problem? No. It is a leadership and formation challenge that looks like a technology problem.  
Is this theological? Yes. Every tool has an embedded worldview. For faith-based organizations, this intersects directly with human dignity and pastoral care.  
Are you partisan, politically or ecclesially? No. We serve orthodox churches across denominations and secular nonprofits united by serious missional constraints.  
What happens when the technology changes? The technology will change weekly. Good policies govern data behavior and human oversight, remaining stable regardless of which LLM wins.

**Who Movemental serves**

Who is this actually for? Leaders responsible for people, mission, and outcomes.  
Is this only for Christian organizations? We primarily serve churches and faith-based nonprofits, but the framework successfully protects any serious mission-driven organization.  
Do you work with small organizations? Yes. Small organizations often need to implement safety the fastest because they lack large IT departments.  
What about denominations and judicatories? Yes. We help networks build baseline policies that their constituent churches can individually adopt.  
Is this for individual leaders or only organizations? The system is built for organizational adoption, though it begins with individual leader clarity.  
Where do movement leaders fit? They are the relational glue guiding this transition. See the leaders on the home page and the Founders screen.

**Ways to engage**

What are the engagement options? Safety Sessions, Guided Pathways, and Tech Partnerships. See Work with Us on the Contact page.  
What is the engagement model? We partner intensively over a set timeline rather than selling ongoing software subscriptions.  
Who needs to attend from our side? Senior leadership for the initial Safety Session; department heads for Sandbox and Training phases.  
Is this virtual or in-person? Typically virtual, though we offer in-person executive retreats for large network adoptions.  
How quickly can we start? Often within two weeks of our initial conversation.  
Can we pause or step out mid-engagement? Yes. The sequence is modular. You can stop after safety is attained and wait until you are ready for step two.

**Cost, time, and the boring questions**

What does this cost? It scales to the size of the organization and the depth of the pathway chosen. Safety sessions are priced accessibly so no organization remains exposed.  
Can you give a budget range? We provide specific ranges on our initial diagnostic call based on your organizational complexity. Every price is on the Pricing page.  
Do you offer reduced rates for smaller organizations? Yes. We reserve capacity for sliding-scale interventions for high-impact, low-resource nonprofits.  
How long does an engagement take? A paid Safety step takes two weeks start to finish with us, or about one to two months self-paced on your own. Training runs eight weeks online. Sandbox and Tech are scoped to your organization.  
Will this slow our team down? In the short term, yes. Wisdom is slower than recklessness. In the long term, it creates massive acceleration through clarity.  
What time commitment do our leaders need? Four to six hours of focused synchronous time over the first month.  
Who pays for tools and vendors? We do not resell. You pay software vendors directly, guaranteeing we have no perverse incentives.

**Tools, data, and the safety boundary**

Do you recommend specific tools? Yes, but strictly relative to your established data boundaries and acceptable use policy.  
Do you have a vendor relationship with ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, or Gemini? No. We remain strictly agnostically independent.  
What data should never enter an AI tool? Unless you have a zero-retention enterprise agreement, PII, pastoral counseling notes, payroll data, and proprietary intellectual property must be locked out.  
Do you build custom assistants? Yes, during the Tech stage, but only after clear review rules are defined and tested.  
Who owns what we produce together? You own all contextual policies and architectures we draft together.  
What about data privacy and security? Data security is the literal purpose of starting our sequence with Safety.

**Voices, evidence, and credibility**

What is the difference between Voices and Evidence? Evidence explains the problem structure; Voices are the practitioners validating it, the movement leaders behind the path.  
Where are your case studies? Named case studies are in development. In the meantime: the field guides (what we teach), the movement leaders directory (who stand alongside this work), and the founders' longer arc on About. Specific named clients come once we have permission to publish them, not before.  
Why doesn't your site have a logo wall? We do not show client logos without explicit permission, and the kind of trust this work requires is not transferred by brand association. The proof is whether the work actually holds up.  
Who counts as a "voice"? Active, missional practitioners who prioritize human formation over simple organizational scaling.  
Can we talk to a current partner? Yes. Once an engagement scope is defined, we are happy to provide references.

**What we will not do** — quoted under item 11.

**What happens after the engagement**

What do we walk away with? Written policies, trained staff, safe sandboxes, and clear alignment across the organization. You walk away with capacity.  
What happens after Safety? You are free to safely experiment inside structured Sandboxes, once your AI Charter is ratified.  
Do we have an ongoing relationship with Movemental after the engagement? We offer retention and advisory availability for previous pathway clients to assist with subsequent vendor evaluations.  
What if our team changes mid-engagement or after? Because we have written the policies down, new team members can be onboarded to the system seamlessly.  
Where do we go if we still have questions? Use the contact form on our Contact page. We answer every message personally.

**Still needed:** expand each answer to 60–150 words. Add the awkward one the checklist names: why a small church pays the same as a denomination — only after item 14 (access mechanism) is written, so the answer is true.

## Personas (from the checklist)

**01 · The checker** · Evaluator · absorbs the backer  
Wants: to know whether the person behind the company is real, and whether they would be embarrassed to have backed, booked, or hired him.  
Needs: one place where you paid a cost. A specific moment where being honest was expensive and you were honest anyway. Second: speed. The verdict has to be available in ninety seconds.  
Loses them: corporate polish that hides the person. An unlinked claim. A superlative. Anything that reads as optimized.

**02 · The builder** · Learner · highest volume, reachable cold  
Wants: your stack, your method, and the how.  
Needs: the judgment, not the stack. The stack is obsolete in eight months. What transfers is how you decided: when to stop, what you refused to automate, how you knew the output was wrong when it looked right. Second: permission to be at the floor.  
Loses them: hype. Gatekeeping. A walkthrough where nothing broke.

**03 · The leader** · Leader · absorbs the peer, network-warm  
Wants: trustworthy thinking on leading with AI, from someone who has built it and understands their world.  
Needs: to find out their organization has already decided. Second: someone who will not flatter them.  
Loses them: techno-optimism that skips formation. Being talked down to. Any sense that the essay is a funnel.

## 01 · Person layer · The arc, told once, canonically

- **Required.** Type: Narrative page. Length: 1,200–1,800. Location: `/about`.
- **Status:** Attached, thin. Live `/about` is ~750–800 words. Longer draft: `docs/article-export/00-preface-the-story.md` (~4,070 words) — candidate to expand `/about` or to publish as a thinking piece, not a second arc.

### Attached — live `/about` (full)

I came to technology through mission, and I have never really left either one.

**One. Roots in direct service.**  
I started in rooms where the work was obviously real. Meals, housing paperwork, teenagers who needed an adult to show up on a Tuesday. Nothing about it was abstract, and nobody in those rooms cared what I thought about systems.

What I learned there is the thing I keep coming back to. The bottleneck was almost never willingness. It was that the organization could not remember what it had already figured out, so every good idea got reinvented at half strength by someone who did not know it had been tried.

**Two. A call, and a community.**  
Then a decision I would not describe as a career move. I joined a community that sent people, and I went. Several years, several countries, a lot of it unglamorous and some of it genuinely hard.

I mention it because it explains the rest. I am not a technologist who found a market in mission organizations. I am someone from those organizations who learned to build.

Pull quote: I am not a technologist who found a market in mission organizations. I am someone from those organizations who learned to build.

**Three. Learning to build.**  
Badly, at first, and in public. I taught myself because the tools we needed did not exist at a price anyone I worked with could pay, and because waiting for someone else to make them was not working.

For a long time this was a hobby that kept becoming useful. I would build something small to solve a problem in front of me, and then three other people would want it, and then it would break in a way I did not understand.

**Four. The hinge.**  
Then building software got cheap. Not free, and not easy, but cheap enough that the constraint moved. For fifteen years the question had been whether a thing could be built at all by people like us. Now it is what is worth building, which is a much harder question and a much better one.

This is the hinge the whole site turns on. I do not think most organizations have understood yet that the expensive part has moved.

Pull quote: The constraint moved from building the thing to knowing what is worth building.

**Five. Two people, not a product.**  
Movemental is two people. It is not a startup with a roadmap and a growth target, and I am wary of describing it as one, because that framing would change what we say yes to.

Being small is not a virtue by itself. It just means the constraints are honest. We cannot take work we do not believe in to keep a team employed, which is a luxury, and it is also the only reason the rest of this page can be written the way it is.

**Six. The conviction.**  
Authorship can survive this. Not by refusing the machine and not by pretending it is neutral, but by keeping the line between what a person decided and what a system produced visible at every step, to everyone, including the person.

That is not a sentiment. It is a design constraint, and it is testable. Either you can point at a piece of work and say who decided what, or you cannot.

Pull quote: Either you can point at a piece of work and say who decided what, or you cannot.

**The disclosure** — see item 03.

**Selected work.** Evaluators looking for proof of craft should start with the work index and the commitments — not a résumé of logos.  
The work · Movemental · Commitments.

**What I will not do** (short list; full page is item 02)  
I will not publish anything under my name that I did not decide the shape of.  
I will not build a system that speaks in someone's voice without their standing agreement.  
I will not recommend software when the honest answer is a habit.  
I will not take work where I cannot say plainly what I stand to gain.  
I will not put a number on a page that I cannot source.

Kansas City, 2026.

Every serious concern about AI — technical, economic, ethical — eventually collapses into a quieter one: *what does it mean to be human now?*

## 02 · Person layer · The refusals, as a standing page

- **Required.** Type: Commitments page. Length: 400–700. Location: `/refusals` · linked sitewide.
- **Status:** Attached. Live at `/ai-commitments` (~600 words). Rename or alias to `/refusals`; do not write a second page.

### Attached — full live page

What I will not do

Six commitments and one conflict. The commitments are refusals, because a refusal is checkable and a value is not. The conflict is at the foot, at full length.

**One.** I will not manufacture urgency or scarcity.  
No countdowns, no closing-soon cohorts, no limited seats that are not limited, no fear that the reader will be left behind. The pressure to move fast on AI is doing real damage to organizations that should be moving carefully, and any part I played in that would be a contribution to the problem I claim to be solving.

**Two.** I will not fake authorship, mine or anyone's.  
Everything published under my name here, I decided the shape of and wrote the sentences of. Where a machine helped, the provenance line on that piece says what it did. I will not build a system that writes in a living person's voice without their standing, revocable agreement, and I have turned down paid work to keep that.

**Three.** AI never does discernment or care.  
It can retrieve, draft, check, and argue with me. It does not decide who is ready for something, who needs a call rather than an email, or what a person can bear to hear this week. Those are the parts that matter most and they are not slow because we lack tooling. They are slow because attention takes time.

**Four.** I will not make a claim I have not earned.  
Every number on this site resolves to a source, and where a figure cannot be published I say that plainly instead of giving a range that sounds precise. I do not claim outcomes I did not measure, and I do not describe a pilot as a transformation. When I get something wrong I correct it on the page, dated, rather than quietly.

**Five.** Extra care wherever vulnerable people are involved.  
Much of my work sits near organizations serving people in hard circumstances. Their stories are not case study material, their data does not go into a system to make a demo better, and a model does not touch a record about a named individual in a service context. Where I am unsure, the answer is no, and the cost of that falls on me rather than on them.

**Six.** I will not sell software where the honest answer is a habit.  
Most organizations that come to me need to write things down and give one person responsibility for keeping them current. That is free. Saying so costs me revenue in the short run and it is the only version of this work I can defend, because the alternative is selling a tool into a vacuum where it will fail and be blamed for failing.

**The conflict, in full** — see item 03.

Link this page sitewide. It is the checker's fastest read.

### Attached — opening of “My 2025 with AI” (candidate piece 1)

File: `docs/article-export/11-my-2025-with-ai.md`

It was late. The kind of late where the screen is brighter than the room and your eyes start to lie about how much sense a paragraph makes.

I was not staring at a novel problem of philosophy. I was staring at a dashboard, a backlog, and the sickening feeling that I had mistaken velocity for progress. Again.

If you have ever built anything ambitious with AI at your elbow, you might know the feeling I started calling **AI psychosis**—not a clinical diagnosis, just a blunt name for a common delusion: the sense that you are *almost done*, perpetually at eighty percent, while the remaining twenty percent keeps shape-shifting into another eighty. The tool rewards motion. Your nervous system interprets motion as arrival. It is not.

This chapter is the centerpiece case study I promised you—not because my year was the most important year in AI, and not because you should copy my stack. It is here because **credibility books fail when they float above practice**. You deserve to see what the framework looks like when it gets mud on it.

I will tell you the truth as I know it. I will not turn it into a sales pitch.

**Still needed:** three pieces, one build each, chronological, containing the break and the cost, ending in one thing a stranger can check. Do not combine SpecChem, Alan, Brad, and Youthfront in one piece.

### Attached — definitional openings already written (use these as the quotable first answer)

**Fragmentation** — from live About (Movemental) and Josh home:

A leader's life-work, or an institution's, was whole in the living of it. Then it scattered. Into books and talks and decks and inboxes and a few people's memories. Most of it is real, and almost none of it is gathered. That is fragmentation, and it was a quiet problem until AI arrived.

A PDF of a book is closer to a photograph of a book than to the book. You can open it and read it, so it seems obvious a computer has it too. But the words are marks positioned for a human eye.

A talk is an hour nobody wrote down. An article on a site that closed is gone. So a thirty-year body of work is not one body of work. It is four or five that cannot talk to each other.

Authorship can survive this. Not by refusing the machine and not by pretending it is neutral, but by keeping the line between what a person decided and what a system produced visible at every step, to everyone, including the person.

### Attached — terms already defined in live copy (seed the glossary)

**Fragmentation.** A leader's life-work, or an institution's, was whole in the living of it. Then it scattered. Into books and talks and decks and inboxes and a few people's memories. Most of it is real, and almost none of it is gathered.

**Authorship (visible).** Keeping the line between what a person decided and what a system produced visible at every step, to everyone, including the person.

**Formation.** Training transfers technique. Formation reshapes judgment. Information can be structured. Formation requires relationship.

**Provenance.** Every claim on this page is either sourced, marked as a [gap], or marked as opinion (°). Nothing is decorative.

**Refusal (vs value).** The commitments are refusals, because a refusal is checkable and a value is not.

### Other Josh live copy worth attaching (not a checklist item, but usable)

**Home hero.** Kansas City. Building with this since 30 November 2022.  
I help people with AI.

**Situations.**  
movement authors whose life's work is trapped in incompatible formats — Thirty years of writing you cannot search. I build the system that answers from their own words — source attached — and says so when it does not have the material.  
nonprofit teams already using AI with no shared lines — The tools are inside. Nobody has decided what they may touch. I help them write the lines, train the people, and put tools last on purpose.  
practitioners training leaders from impression, not place — Neighborhood work needs something checkable. I build tools that read a place from public sources before anyone plans from vibe.  
organizations whose words still have to mean something — Cheap fluency no longer proves formation. I build the systems and train the people who have to live with what those systems do to judgment.

**Organizations `/organizations`.**  
Movemental. A two-person company building the context layer this site keeps arguing organizations need. This page explains it. It does not sell it.

What it is. Movemental builds and maintains shared context layers for organizations whose work depends on what they already know. In practice that means the boring, load-bearing part: getting what a group has decided into a form a person can find and a system can use, and then keeping it current as the group keeps deciding things.

We sell engagements, not seats. An engagement is usually a bounded pilot on one real workstream, with stated success and failure criteria, and it either proves something or it ends.

The company is small on purpose. Two people cannot take work they do not believe in to keep a payroll running, and that constraint is the reason I can write the rest of this site the way I do.

Who leads it, and why. I am the founder and the CTO. My co-founder holds the CEO seat, and that was a deliberate handoff rather than a formality or a title swap.

If I were the CEO, everything I published would be marketing, whatever I intended. The separation is real — see the commitments page.

If you want to work with the company, that conversation starts at movemental.ai, not here.

**AI Lab about.**  
How the Lab works, and what it won't do.

The Lab is retrieval with receipts, not a persona. It searches things I have written and built on this site, quotes them, and cites the page each quote came from.

It will not speak as me, or invent a position I have not published.  
It will not manufacture urgency, scarcity, or a claim I have not earned.  
It will not touch a record about a named individual in a service context.
